blocks.prompt: 2. Find the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the arithmetic-geometric sequence, where the arithmetic part is \(3, 7, 11, \ldots\) and the geometric part is \(2, 6, 18, \ldots\)
blocks.explanation:
Same idea as Question 1, but now the term number is a general \(n\).
Plan: write the \(n\)th term of the A.P. and of the G.P. in terms of \(n\), then multiply and simplify.
steps:
Given: A.P. part \(3, 7, 11, \ldots\) (\(a = 3, d = 4\)); G.P. part \(2, 6, 18, \ldots\) (\(b = 2, r = 3\))
To find: the \(n\)th term \(T_n\).
Method: The \(n\)th term of an A.G.P. is (\(n\)th term of the A.P. part) \(\times\) (\(n\)th term of the G.P. part): \(T_n = [a + (n - 1)d]\,br^{n-1}\).

\(n\)th term of the A.P. part
\[a_n = 3 + (n - 1)(4)\]
\[= 3 + 4n - 4\]
\[= 4n - 1\]
Why: \(d = 7 - 3 = 4\); open the bracket and collect the numbers.

\(n\)th term of the G.P. part
\[b_n = 2 \cdot 3^{n-1}\]
Why: \(r = 6/2 = 3\) and \(b_n = br^{n-1}\).

Multiply
\[T_n = (4n - 1) \cdot 2 \cdot 3^{n-1}\]
\[= 2(4n - 1)\,3^{n-1}\]
Why: The A.G.P. term is the product; the constant 2 is written in front.

Check with \(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\)
\[T_1 = 2(3)(3^{0}) = 6 = 3 \times 2\]
\[T_2 = 2(7)(3) = 42 = 7 \times 6\]
Why: Both agree with multiplying the first and second terms of the two parts.
